memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abram, saying, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth." - Gen 14:18-19 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Out of nowhere steps one of the most mysterious figures in all of Scripture. Melchizedek - king of Salem (which means peace) and "priest of God Most High." He appears without genealogy, without introduction, brings out bread and wine, and blesses Abram. Then he vanishes from the story.

Notice what he combines: he is both king and priest. In Israel's later history, those offices were strictly separate - kings from Judah's line, priests from Levi's. But here, before either existed, stands a man who is both, blessing the father of the faith.

The New Testament tells us who this points to. Hebrews devotes chapters to Melchizedek, showing that Jesus is "a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek" (Heb 7:17) - a priest-king whose office does not come through Levi's line but by God's own appointment. Melchizedek is a signpost, and Christ is the destination.

And the bread and wine? We cannot press it too far, but Christians down the centuries have found it hard to miss. Here is a priest-king of Salem bringing bread and wine and pronouncing blessing - and here is our Priest-King, who took bread and wine and said, "This is my body... this is my blood" (Luke 22:19-20), and who is our peace. Receive today from the King who blesses you freely.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Do you know Jesus as both your King and your Priest?
- What does it mean to simply receive God's blessing rather than earn it?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord Jesus, You are my Priest-King forever, the true King of peace. Thank You for the bread and wine of Your own body and blood. I receive Your blessing today with open hands.
Amen.
